Indeed · Indeed Job Refresh

The job was still open. Its visibility had faded.

Employers recreated jobs to make them look active again. I connected that research finding to a platform initiative and proposed Refresh: support the behavior employers wanted while giving job seekers more current information.

Role
Senior UX Designer
Scope
User testing, cross-team proposal, information architecture, interaction design, messaging, and prototypes
Key decision
Refresh the existing job through meaningful updates instead of recreating it
Outcome
Employers reported less time and effort than closing and reposting

I — Inspiration

Employers were recreating jobs to recover visibility

While I tested applicant-management concepts, employers repeatedly described the same workaround without prompting: close a stale post and recreate the job so it looked active again. They wanted renewed visibility, not another record to manage.

I brought that finding to my product owner and lead engineer. A separate platform initiative was already exploring duplicate reduction. The research gave us a product opportunity alongside that technical work: make maintaining the existing job more useful than recreating it.

Research context: the freemium exploration

The work began with two goals: meet employers’ expectations of a free offering and make additional paid value worth choosing. I proposed a feature inventory and a Kano-based approach to employer expectations, then worked with product and engineering on three prototype directions.

My strategy deck compared seven freemium models using an ice-cream metaphor. We leaned toward Freeware: additions that complement a free core. That framed the research, but Refresh emerged from employers’ unsolicited comments rather than from the model itself.

Applicant search, filtering, and management remained prototype explorations. We paused to consider potential hiring bias. They are context for the research, not delivered outcomes of Refresh.

D — Design Process

Preserve the intent behind the workaround

The issue crossed marketplace boundaries. Duplicate records complicated reporting; stale posts could attract applications after an employer had stopped attending to them. Renewed visibility needed to signal a genuinely active job.

I used prototypes to connect employer intent to that requirement. Refresh would keep the existing record and ask for substantial, recent changes to compensation, the description, or company information. Simply resurfacing an unchanged post would preserve the information problem.

E — Engagement

Address the cause alongside technical cleanup

I connected with the engineers working on the separate duplicate-reduction initiative. They were exploring a technical solution to identify and de-duplicate posts, but identifying true duplicates was difficult. Archiving or merging jobs that were actually distinct was a risk we could not take.

I proposed a complementary path: change the behavior before another duplicate was created. Employers could renew the existing post instead of asking the platform to identify and remove duplicates afterward.

I wrote a proposal deck for my team to collaborate on a solution: offer job-post refreshes on a trial basis, then fold the feature into Sponsored Jobs. The proposal connected employer value, the platform’s data problem, and fresher information signaling that an employer was still actively reviewing applications.

My product owner and lead engineer helped align stakeholders around the proposal. I owned the information architecture, interaction flow, messaging, and prototypes; the wider team carried delivery.

A — Action

Keep the job. Improve the information.

I designed the information architecture, interaction flow, and messaging, using prototypes to make the proposition understandable: update a stale job with meaningful information rather than close it and start again.

Refresh required substantial, recent updates, such as compensation, job-description details, or company information. Renewed visibility had to be connected to more current information. Resurfacing an unchanged listing would have left job seekers with the same potentially outdated description.

S — Success

A benefit employers had already been seeking

The team made Refresh available to a segment of free job posts. Employers gave positive feedback that it saved time and effort compared with closing and reposting. It remained free for six months, then became a Sponsored Jobs feature.

Employer feedback was qualitative. Revenue lift, paid adoption, changes in duplicate-job volume, and job-seeker outcomes are not quantified in this account. The applicant-management tools remained prototype exploration in this story.

My takeaway is to investigate the intent behind a workaround. Employers wanted their jobs to look active; duplication was one way they pursued that goal. Connecting that intent to another team’s constraints let me propose a product path that supported the desired behavior at its source.
